source.title: Gradients explode - Deep Networks are shallow - ResNet explained
source.authors: George Philipp; D. Song; J. Carbonell

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper. Its displayed title differs from the record title: the text is “The exploding gradient problem demystified.”
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains deep MLPs on CIFAR-10 and reports training classification error under varied architectures, initialization, normalization, and step-size recipes. These experiments bear on several versions, but do not use the versions’ original convolutional, benchmark, or optimization setups.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own CIFAR-10 training results and its explicit minibatch failure for batch-ReLU. The Gaussian-noise initialization measurements are not training-error results and are not rows. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study tests initialization-dependent trainability (V4) and batch normalization's optimization benefit (V6) in deep CIFAR-10 MLPs. It does not test convolutional memorization (V1), teacher-student minima (V2), degradation across trained depths (V3), or stability-threshold dynamics (V5).
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct, but should distinguish orthogonal initial functions from merely orthogonal weight matrices. The authors argue that exploding relative gradients and collapsing domains constrain effective depth; shortcuts and looks-linear initialization reduce these pathologies. Layer-wise step sizes strongly affect outcomes but do not consistently improve them. They do not claim normalization or careful variance scaling generally solves the problem.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains fully connected MLPs with SGD on CIFAR-10 to study gradient pathology and effective depth. It does not reproduce the cited convolutional-network classification recipes; it varies layer types, initialization, normalization, skip connections, and step-size choices.
record.method_sensitivity: Training error varies with architecture, normalization, initialization, skip connections, and whether step sizes are custom layer-wise or shared. For batch-ReLU, minibatches versus full-batch training also changes whether learning occurs.

fits_no_version.finding: Identity-skip residual MLPs generally attain lower error than corresponding vanilla MLPs at the same compositional depth; layer-SELU is an exception.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed depth, residual shortcuts generally improve optimization of the tested deep MLP architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Initialization-state GSC, effective depth, and Taylor-reduction robustness reveal gradient and co-adaptation pathologies, but are not themselves training-speed or depth-degradation measurements.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Exploding relative gradients and collapsing domains can constrain useful updates and effective co-adaptation in deep MLPs.

fits_no_version.finding: Several MLP configurations attain near-zero CIFAR-10 training error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some 51-layer, width-100 MLP recipes fit ordinary CIFAR-10 labels nearly perfectly.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Learning Representations (listed in record; paper text says “Editor: TBD”)
record.problems: Experiments are limited to MLPs and CIFAR-10. No CIFAR-100, corrupted-label, or convolutional experiments are reported. The authors note custom step-size selection is noisy and complex, and that their effective-depth estimate has limitations. No uncertainty intervals are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional training-error rows omitted. Gaussian-noise measurements, initialization-state GSC values, and Taylor-depth-reduction results were excluded because they are not separate training classification error outcomes bearing directly on these versions.

untested.parts: All: no convolutional networks, CIFAR-100, corrupted-label experiments, or tests of sufficient convolutional model size.
All: no two-layer teacher-student problem, spurious-minimum frequencies, or extra-neuron intervention.
No comparison of separately trained shallower and deeper networks, no convolutional degradation experiment, and no special deep-tanh or Fixup recipe.
No training-speed comparison of orthogonal versus Gaussian tanh weights at equal variance, no convolutional kernels or 10,000-layer training, and no empirical sweep of trainable depth.
All: no initial linearized stability threshold, squared-loss catapult experiment, or sharpness trajectory relative to the stability threshold.
Higher-learning-rate tolerance, the named original architectures and datasets, and Fixup are untested. Endpoint rows generally do not determine accuracy-gain speed.

missing.what: The orthogonal, unnormalized ReLU initialization control reaches 12.51% error with a single step size, versus Gaussian ReLU's 19.24% and looks-linear ReLU's 0.008%. It distinguishes ordinary orthogonal weights from looks-linear initialization.

record.verdict_notes: All supplied training-error values match Table 2. R1/R9, R2/R4/R10 are duplicates. Results are selected after recipe searches, not averages with uncertainty intervals. Rows linked to both V4 and V6 have an observed state only for the initialization comparison; their endpoint values cannot establish V6 acceleration. No verdict is withheld because of original-source status: this study is not among the listed originals.

versions.untested_parts: Tests MLPs on CIFAR-10 with ordinary labels. Does not test convolutional networks, CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, Adam, smaller-model comparisons, or early stopping.

Compares vanilla MLP architectures with MLP ResNet architectures on CIFAR-10. Does not test batch-normalized convolutional networks, ImageNet, or the cited special initialization for very deep plain tanh networks.

Compares Gaussian, orthogonal, and looks-linear initialization in MLPs on CIFAR-10. Does not test activation-matched initialization broadly, orthogonal convolution kernels, or trainability at 10,000 layers.
Tests normalization variants in MLPs on CIFAR-10, including a minibatch failure and full-batch batch-ReLU training. Does not test sigmoid MNIST, VGG CIFAR-10, Inception ImageNet, or Fixup.

relation.reason: Its own CIFAR-10 training experiments compare initialization schemes and normalization conditions, bearing directly on V4 and V6.

tranche.reason: The study supplies an explicit counterargument and empirical failure condition for normalization's optimization benefit: minibatch batch-ReLU essentially does not learn, and adding normalization introduces the gradient pathology. T5 captures this qualification more specifically than a new-setting designation.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is titled The exploding gradient problem demystified and is arXiv v4 dated April 2018; the pack uses an earlier title and year. Endpoint errors support initialization-dependent trainability, but do not independently measure training acceleration or higher-learning-rate tolerance.

statements.correction: Table 2: single-step-size Gaussian versus looks-linear errors are 19.24% versus 0.008% without normalization and 21.23% versus 1.2% with layer normalization. H.4: CIFAR-10 training set; SGD; matched step-size selection procedure. Supplied header: arXiv v4, 6 April 2018; Editor TBD; peer-review status unverified.
statements.problem: The experimental comparisons are correct, but the supplied text does not establish the asserted reviewed status.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: 51-layer-width-100 MLPs trained on CIFAR-10 with ordinary labels
reader_labels.reason: Most Gaussian-initialized vanilla results remain well above zero, while SELU and looks-linear initialization achieve low errors; identity-skip ResNets also reach low error (R1–R2, R5–R24, R25–R34). The minibatch batch-ReLU run makes essentially no learning progress (R3). This is not the version’s convolutional or random-label setting.
